relationship: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo simulates Hamilton's equations (a first-order ODE system) to propose samples. Langevin dynamics $d\theta = \nabla\log p(\theta \mid x)\,dt + \sqrt 2\,dW$ is a stochastic ODE whose stationary distribution is the target posterior. The deterministic ODE theory developed there is the first-principles foundation for these samplers.

HMC and the No-U-Turn Sampler require evaluating $\nabla_\theta \log p(\theta \mid x) = -\nabla U(\theta)$ at every leapfrog half-step (§26.4); Langevin MCMC uses the gradient of the log-density as a drift term. Gradient availability is the practical distinction between HMC and random-walk Metropolis; volume preservation (Proof 3) uses the Jacobian determinant of the leapfrog map.

Non-centered parameterization $\theta = \mu + \sigma \cdot z$ with $z \sim N(0, 1)$ decouples the posterior geometry of hierarchical models; the reparameterization introduces a trivial Jacobian ($\sigma$) making the sampler more efficient. Volume preservation of leapfrog integration in HMC is a Jacobian-determinant-equals-1 statement.

Gaussian state-space models $dx = Ax\,dt + dW$ are linear stochastic ODEs. The Kalman filter is the exact posterior recursion for such systems, and HMC for Gaussian targets is a linear Hamiltonian ODE whose trajectories preserve the target measure.

Convergence rates of MCMC are metric-space statements: the chain converges to its stationary distribution in total-variation or Wasserstein distance. Contraction-mapping arguments (coupling) give geometric convergence rates for the §26.7 Markov-chain ergodic theorem.

MCMC is a strategy for approximating $d$-dimensional integrals when $d$ is too large for deterministic quadrature. The target is always an expectation $\int g(\theta)\,p(\theta \mid x)\,d\theta$, and the sampler converts this into an ergodic-average approximation.

The leapfrog integrator in HMC is a second-order symplectic numerical ODE scheme. Its volume-preservation and reversibility are exactly the properties that make HMC's Metropolis–Hastings correction a Bernoulli variable with computable acceptance probability; step-size tuning is the bias–cost tradeoff familiar from numerical ODE analysis.

The posterior $p(\theta \mid x) = p(x \mid \theta)\pi(\theta) / \int p(x \mid \theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$ has an integral normalizing constant; Bayesian estimators, credible intervals, and posterior predictives are all posterior expectations — hence integrals. MCMC is fundamentally an integral-approximation method; §26.7 frames ergodic averages as Cesàro time-averaging of the invariant-measure integral, and the Kac formula (Proof 4 Step 3) is a stopping-time integration argument.

Ergodicity of a Markov chain — convergence of the chain to its stationary distribution regardless of starting point — is the discrete-time analog of global stability of a dynamical system. Spectral-gap analysis (second-largest eigenvalue of the transition operator) mirrors linear stability analysis of ODE equilibria.

VI is the non-MCMC alternative for approximate posterior inference: pick a tractable q(θ), minimize KL(q ∥ p(· | y)). Trades exactness for speed. §26.10 Rem 26 names the contrast; formalml develops ELBO, mean-field, and normalizing flows.

SGLD (Welling–Teh 2011) and SGHMC (Chen–Fox–Guestrin 2014) replace the full-batch gradient in HMC / Langevin with a mini-batch gradient plus injected noise. Scales MCMC to large-n datasets at the cost of introducing asymptotic bias. §26.10 Rem 30.
SMC / particle filters are the alternative when the target is a sequence π_t indexed by time or annealing parameter. Parallel to MCMC's single-target framework. §26.10 Rem 31.
Stan, PyMC, NumPyro — domain-specific languages that compile user-specified models into NUTS samplers. Topic 26 motivates; formalml explores the compiler stack. §26.10 Rem 33.

The standard Metropolis–Hastings framework and detailed-balance machinery of §26 is the foundation that RJ-MCMC's §§4 and 7 extend to trans-dimensional moves. §26.10 Remark 28 forward-pointed at RJ-MCMC; that pointer is discharged on the formalml side.

RMHMC is a direct extension of the HMC treatment in §26.9–10, discharging §26.10 Remark 29's forward pointer to Riemannian-manifold methods. The canonical-distribution construction, leapfrog integrator, and Metropolis correction developed here are assumed by RMHMC.

The NUTS sampler and ADVI machinery introduced in this topic underwrite §4's PyMC fits in stacking-and-predictive-ensembles, and §6.1's computational-averaging use case is a topic-level application of MCMC variability across chains and approximate-inference methods.

§9's annealed importance sampling in variational-bayes-for-model-selection is MCMC machinery — AIS uses Metropolis–Hastings transitions between intermediate distributions, and the schedule-length convergence argument depends on the MCMC ergodicity vocabulary developed in this topic.

§25.8 Proof 3 (BvM sketch) Taylor-expands the log-posterior in a neighborhood of $\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}$; the leading Gaussian term is extracted via standard Taylor-with-remainder. The Laplace approximation remark is multivariate Taylor with a Hessian determinant.

§25.7 Rem on reparameterization invariance of Jeffreys prior uses the Jacobian change-of-variables formula to show $\pi_J(\phi) = \pi_J(\theta)|d\theta/d\phi|$ for any monotone reparameterization $\phi = g(\theta)$.

Gaussian-process priors over functions are specified by a mean and covariance kernel — a Hilbert-space structure. The Cameron–Martin space associated with a GP prior is the RKHS of the kernel; posterior contractions happen in this Hilbert-space geometry, which is what the formalcalculus hilbert-spaces topic underwrites.

Conjugate priors (Beta–Binomial, Gamma–Poisson, Normal–Normal) are constructed so the posterior normalizer reduces to a ratio of Gamma or Beta functions. Improper priors (Jeffreys, flat) require the improper-integral machinery to verify posterior propriety.

The marginal likelihood $m(\mathbf{y}) = \int L(\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$ and posterior predictive $p(\tilde y \mid \mathbf{y}) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)p(\theta \mid \mathbf{y})\,d\theta$ are integrals against the prior / posterior density over the full parameter space. In $d$ dimensions Fubini justifies iterated computation; §25.4 Proof 1 closes the conjugate-family case by identifying the integrand's kernel with a known density family.

Posterior densities $p(\theta \mid x)$ are Radon–Nikodym derivatives of the posterior measure w.r.t. a dominating measure (Lebesgue on $\mathbb R^d$, counting on a countable set). Likelihoods $L(\theta; x)$ are RN derivatives of the data measure across different $\theta$; Bayes' rule is a change-of-measure identity.

BNN posteriors are MVN near the MAP estimate by BvM (§25.8 Thm 5); the Laplace approximation (§25.8 Rem 16) is the canonical construction. formalml's BNN topic develops non-conjugate posterior approximation via variational inference, extending Topic 25's Laplace machinery to deep-network-scale models.

When conjugate priors break down (non-exponential-family likelihoods, hierarchical models beyond Topic 28) and MCMC is too slow, variational inference approximates the posterior with a tractable family $q(\theta)$ minimizing $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p(\cdot \mid \mathbf{y}))$. Topic 25 §25.10 pointers; formalml develops ELBO, mean-field VI, normalizing flows.

GPs are the infinite-dimensional generalization of Topic 25's finite-dimensional Bayesian framework: the prior is over functions rather than parameters, and the posterior is a conditional MVN (Topic 8 Thm 3 applied infinite-dimensionally).

Probabilistic programming languages (Stan, PyMC, NumPyro) automate the posterior computation Topic 25 does by hand — users specify prior × likelihood, the language handles sampling via HMC/NUTS. Topic 25's conjugate calculations show what the PPL would output for the easy cases.

§25.3 Thm 1 (posterior $\propto$ prior $\times$ likelihood) is the framework mixed-effects §5's PyMC fit operates inside; §25.5–§25.7's prior-selection theory — conjugate, weakly-informative, and Jeffreys — supplies the menu §5.1 chooses from on variance-component hyperparameters. §25.7's improper-prior theory contains the flat-improper case mixed-effects §4.2 marginalizes over the fixed effects to recover the REML profile likelihood.

Sparse priors are downstream of the prior-elicitation framework developed in this topic. §6's $m_0$ hyperparameter (regularized horseshoe's prior expected number of effective coefficients) and §8's $(a, b, \xi)$ hyperprior on R2-D2 are concrete elicitations of the §25.5 weakly-informative prior class.

Develops prior elicitation; §4.1's four candidate priors (weakly informative Gaussians, half-Normal scales, inverse-gamma length scales) build directly on the §25.5–§25.7 elicitation framework, and §6.1's sensitivity-analysis use case is the topic-level application.

VBMS is downstream of the prior–likelihood–posterior decomposition and depends critically on hyperprior choice. §4's Bayesian-GMM ARD result is sensitive to the Dirichlet concentration $\alpha$; §11's computational notes return to prior-sensitivity diagnostics.

The Laplace expansion of $m(\mathbf{y}) = \int L(\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$ uses multivariate Gaussian integration over a neighborhood of the posterior mode. §27.6 Proof 2 cites this mechanism directly.

Second-order Taylor expansion of $\log L(\theta)\pi(\theta)$ around $\hat\theta$ is the analytical backbone of the Occam–BIC equivalence (§27.6 Proof 2). Laplace approximation Taylor-expands the log-posterior to second order around the MAP; the resulting Gaussian approximation has covariance $(-\nabla^2\ell)^{-1}$, and the BIC asymptotic derivation rests on the higher-order error term of this expansion.

Laplace approximation: $\int \exp(\ell(\theta))\,d\theta \approx \exp(\ell(\hat\theta)) \cdot (2\pi)^{d/2} \cdot |\det(-\nabla^2\ell(\hat\theta))|^{-1/2}$. The determinant of the Hessian at the MAP is the volume correction; BIC $= -2\,\ell(\hat\theta) + d\log n$ is the asymptotic form of this expansion.

The Laplace approximation $\int \exp(\ell(\theta))\,d\theta \approx \exp(\ell(\hat\theta)) \cdot (2\pi)^{d/2}/\sqrt{\det(-\nabla^2\ell(\hat\theta))}$ is a second-order Taylor expansion of the log-posterior around the MAP. The BIC penalty falls out of this expansion, and the mean-value-theorem remainder bound controls the asymptotic accuracy.

SMC samplers yield an unbiased estimator of the marginal likelihood $m(\mathbf{y}) = \int L(\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta$ as a side product (Del Moral–Doucet–Jasra 2006 Proposition 1) — the canonical alternative to bridge sampling and harmonic-mean estimators in §27's model-evidence catalogue. formalml/sequential-monte-carlo §8.2's Theorem 4 is the formal statement; §8.4's GMM benchmark is the empirical comparison. (Note: the estimator of $\log m(\mathbf{y})$ obtained by taking the logarithm is generally biased by Jensen's inequality; Proposition 1's unbiasedness is for the normalizing-constant estimate, not its log.)

Stacking is the M-open alternative to BMA: optimize predictive weights directly rather than derive them from marginal likelihoods. Critical when no candidate model is true. §27.10 Rem 26 sets up the contrast.

The evidence lower bound (ELBO) is a variational approximation to $\log m(\mathbf{y})$ derived from the Kullback–Leibler projection of the posterior onto a tractable family. Replaces MCMC+bridge for very large models at the cost of approximation bias.

RJMCMC (Green 1995) samples directly from the joint posterior over $(\mathcal{M}_k, \theta_k)$, providing BMA weights as a byproduct. An alternative to separate marginal-likelihood estimates when the model space is discrete and structured.

The Monte-Carlo error in §31.2 hinges on the $B \to \infty$ limit of the empirical average $B^{-1}\sum g(X^\ast_{(b)})$ to its conditional expectation — sequence-limit machinery from formalcalculus. Bootstrap consistency asserts $\sqrt n(\hat\theta^\ast - \hat\theta) \xrightarrow d$ to the limit law of $\sqrt n(\hat\theta - \theta)$, itself a sequence-limit of empirical measures.

Lemma 1 in §31.3 (Polya's theorem) upgrades pointwise convergence of monotone functions with a continuous limit to uniform convergence. The partition argument is a classical uniform-convergence proof.

The bootstrap approximates the true sampling distribution of an estimator by the bootstrap sampling distribution. The validity proof is an approximation statement: the bootstrap empirical process converges to the same Gaussian limit as the true empirical process, framed via the bracketing/covering apparatus of formalcalculus approximation-theory.

Bootstrap consistency is often stated as $L^2$ convergence of the bootstrap distribution to the true sampling distribution. Moment-matching arguments in second-order bootstrap validity proofs work in $L^2$ — the formalcalculus $L^p$ topic provides the rigorous normed-space substrate.

The Edgeworth expansion of $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta)$ in §31.5 is a Taylor-style series in the characteristic function with coefficients driven by cumulants. Bootstrap higher-order accuracy — $O(n^{-1})$ vs the CLT's $O(n^{-1/2})$ — follows from matching Edgeworth terms between bootstrap and true distributions.

§31.4's bootstrap CIs are the foundation of conformal-prediction's non-residual precursor: construct a bootstrap distribution for the point prediction, then take percentile endpoints as the prediction-interval bounds.

§31.3's Theorem 3 underwrites bootstrapped model uncertainty: bag multiple bootstrap replicates of the training set, refit the model on each, and use the distribution of test-time predictions as a proxy for posterior uncertainty.

Bootstrap and permutation are both resampling-based approaches to inference but differ in their null-hypothesis treatment. Bootstrap resamples with replacement under the empirical distribution (no symmetry assumption); permutation resamples without replacement under exchangeability. §31.10 Rem 24 contrasts the two; rank-tests develops the permutation side.
Pointwise limits of MGFs and characteristic functions, limsup in Berry–Esseen rate analysis.
Taylor series and power series expansions are the backbone of the MGF proof: log(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + O(x³) applied with x = O(1/n).
Taylor's theorem with remainder provides the rigorous bound on the remainder term in the MGF expansion. The delta method requires differentiability of the transformation g.

Characteristic functions $\varphi_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{itX}]$ are Fourier transforms of densities; Lévy's continuity theorem (convergence of characteristic functions implies convergence in distribution) is an application of Fourier inversion. The CLT is cleanest to prove on the Fourier side via Taylor expansion of $\log\varphi$.

The characteristic-function proof of the CLT expands $\log\varphi_X(t)$ to second order in $t$ near 0: $\log\varphi_X(t) = i\mu t - \sigma^2 t^2/2 + o(t^2)$. Summing and rescaling gives the Gaussian characteristic function in the limit — pure Taylor expansion with an MVT-controlled remainder.

The characteristic-function proof of the CLT expands $\log\varphi_{X_i}(t/\sqrt n)$ as a Taylor series in $t$. The dominant terms give the Gaussian characteristic function $e^{-\sigma^2 t^2/2}$; the remainder terms vanish as $n \to \infty$ at rate set by the Berry–Esseen third-moment bound.

The mini-batch gradient is an average of $B$ iid gradient samples; by the CLT, its fluctuations around the true gradient are Gaussian at scale $\sigma/\sqrt B$, which motivates the learning-rate schedule $\eta \propto 1/\sqrt t$ and explains why larger batches reduce noise with diminishing returns.

Rademacher complexity bounds use symmetrization and CLT-type reasoning. The empirical Rademacher complexity converges to its expectation at rate $1/\sqrt n$, giving the $O(1/\sqrt n)$ generalization bound for bounded loss functions.

The Bernstein–von Mises theorem (the Bayesian CLT) proves that the posterior $\sqrt n(\theta - \theta_0) \mid X_1, \ldots, X_n$ converges in total variation to $N(0, I(\theta_0)^{-1})$, where $I(\theta_0)$ is the Fisher information — why Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals agree asymptotically.

Required for the asymptotic null distributions throughout rank-tests: the normal approximation to $W^+$ in §1, $U$ in §3, and the multivariate finite-population CLT (Hájek 1960) that powers §4's chi-squared limit. §5's Pitman ARE proof leans on the joint CLT under contiguous alternatives.
§12's head-to-head benchmark uses Bayesian logistic regression with asymptotically-Gaussian posterior by Bernstein–von Mises; CLT is the underlying mechanism for that asymptotic Gaussianity.
The proof that independence of events implies independence of their complements uses basic algebraic manipulation of limits. The same epsilon-N framework from formalCalculus Topic 1.

The Radon–Nikodym theorem is exactly the existence proof for conditional expectation $\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G]$: given a $\sigma$-finite measure $P$ restricted to $\mathcal G$ and the measure $\nu(A) = \int_A X\,dP$ on $\mathcal G$, the RN derivative $d\nu/dP|_{\mathcal G}$ is $\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G]$. Conditional probability is its special case for indicator integrands.

Conditional expectation $\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G]$ is defined as the unique (a.s.) $\mathcal G$-measurable random variable satisfying $\mathbb E[X \cdot \mathbb 1_A] = \mathbb E[\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G] \cdot \mathbb 1_A]$ for all $A \in \mathcal G$ — a $\sigma$-algebra-level construction. The Radon–Nikodym theorem guarantees its existence.

Conditional entropy H(X|Y) = -Σ P(x,y) log P(x|y) and mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) are defined via conditional probability. The chain rule for entropy H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) mirrors the chain rule for probability.
The posterior distribution P(θ|data) ∝ P(data|θ)P(θ) is Bayes' theorem applied to parameter spaces. Every MCMC algorithm, every variational inference method targets this posterior.
Coverage probability P_θ(θ ∈ C(X)) is an integral of the sampling density over the event {θ ∈ C(X)}. The coverage diagnostic in §19.8 computes this integral numerically for binomial p.
Asymptotic coverage — the statement lim_{n→∞} P_θ(θ ∈ C_n(X)) = 1 − α — is a sequences-limits statement. The Wald-under-coverage-in-small-samples result in §19.5 is its finite-sample companion.

The profile likelihood ℓ_P(θ) = sup_ψ ℓ(θ, ψ) is a composition of an implicit function (ψ̂(θ) solves the nuisance score equation) and the joint likelihood. Differentiation under the sup is the Danskin envelope theorem — cited in §19.7 Rem 15.

Inverting a hypothesis test to construct a confidence interval — $C(x) = \{\theta : \text{test does not reject at } x\}$ — is an implicit-function operation: we solve the equation 'test statistic equals critical value' for $\theta$ as a function of $x$. The inverse-function theorem from formalcalculus is what makes the inverted CI well-defined and smooth.

Wald confidence intervals for the average treatment effect — used throughout §§4, 6, 8, 13 of causal-inference-methods — invoke the test–CI duality of §19.2. §12's Rosenbaum bounds and §9.4's Anderson–Rubin confidence sets for IV are non-Wald CIs constructed via test inversion using the same duality machinery.

Prediction-intervals leans on this topic as the formal foundation for both HL-style test-inversion (§4) and the conformal-quantile threshold (§2.3). The duality between a level-$\alpha$ test and a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence region is the abstract machinery behind every interval construction in that topic.

Rank-tests §6's Hodges–Lehmann distribution-free CI is the test-inversion construction applied to the Wilcoxon test, and Theorem 10's proof is a worked instance of the §19.2 duality machinery. The set-theoretic inversion 'a level-$\alpha$ test inverts to a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence region' is the load-bearing step in proving exact coverage.

Semiparametric-inference §10's Wald confidence intervals from the cross-fit sandwich SE follow the §19.4–§19.6 construction. The duality with hypothesis testing carries over: rejecting $H_0: \psi = \psi_0$ at level $\alpha$ is equivalent to $\psi_0$ not lying in the $(1 - \alpha)$ Wald CI.

The Normal MGF derivation uses 'completing the square' in the exponent, and the Gamma function's properties connect to power-series representations. The exponential series $e^x = \sum x^k/k!$ underwrites the MGF identity $M_X(t) = \sum \mathbb E[X^k]\,t^k/k!$ for distributions with finite moments.

Characteristic functions $\varphi_X(t) = \mathbb E[e^{itX}]$ are Fourier transforms of densities. Lévy's continuity theorem — convergence of characteristic functions implies convergence in distribution — is an application of Fourier inversion, and the Normal characteristic function $e^{-\sigma^2 t^2/2}$ is the cleanest demonstration of the Fourier-side approach.
The Gaussian integral ∫e^{−z²/2}dz = √(2π) ensures the Normal PDF normalizes. The Gamma function satisfies Γ(n) = (n−1)! for positive integers, connecting continuous and discrete.
The Chi-squared distribution arises as Z² for Z~N(0,1), requiring the Jacobian. The Beta-Gamma connection Y₁/(Y₁+Y₂) ~ Beta(α,β) uses a bivariate change of variables.
The Gamma function Γ(α) = ∫₀^∞ t^{α-1}e^{-t}dt and all continuous PDFs on unbounded support are improper integrals.
Normal response → linear regression (identity link). Gamma response → Gamma GLM (log link) for positive-valued outcomes like insurance claims and time durations.
The Normal distribution is the marginal of every finite collection of GP outputs. The GP prior is an infinite-dimensional Gaussian.
Gaussian variational families are the default in VI. The Beta serves as the conjugate prior for Bernoulli likelihood in mean-field approximations.
The standard Normal N(0,I) is the base distribution. The change-of-variables formula transforms it through invertible mappings to model complex densities.
Beta-Bernoulli, Gamma-Poisson, and Normal-Normal are the three canonical conjugate pairs used in Bayesian inference and online learning.
The geometric series ∑r^k = 1/(1−r) and its derivatives are used in Geometric and Negative Binomial moment derivations. The limit (1−λ/n)^n → e^{−λ} drives the Poisson limit theorem.

The exponential power series $e^x = \sum x^k/k!$ verifies that the Poisson PMF sums to 1 and drives MGF derivations for the Poisson distribution. The probability generating function $G_X(s) = \mathbb E[s^X] = \sum p_k s^k$ is a power series whose coefficients are the PMF values.

The probability generating function $G_X(s) = \mathbb E[s^X] = \sum p_k s^k$ is a power series whose coefficients are the PMF values. Moment generating functions and cumulant generating functions are Laurent/Taylor series whose coefficients encode the distribution; series-convergence theory determines their domain.

Logistic regression models Y|X ~ Bernoulli(σ(β^T X)). The natural parameter η = log(p/(1−p)) = β^T X is the log-odds, directly from the exponential family form. Cross-entropy loss is the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood.
Poisson regression (log link, count response) and Negative Binomial regression (overdispersed counts) use these distributions as the response family in GLMs.
Bernoulli Naive Bayes models binary feature vectors as independent Bernoulli random variables given the class label.

Pointwise vs uniform convergence of function sequences is the analytic backbone of every §32 theorem; §32.1 opens with that contrast, and Donsker's theorem (§32.5) is the infinite-dimensional limit statement that lifts pointwise sequence-convergence theory to function-valued sequences via tightness and finite-dimensional convergence.

Bracketing numbers and covering numbers — approximation-theoretic measures of the 'size' of a function class — control the uniform convergence rate $\sqrt n(P_n - P)$ over function classes. Donsker classes are exactly those whose bracketing integral converges; the §32.6 use of metric-entropy vocabulary is built on the formalcalculus approximation-theory topic.

The empirical process $X_n: \mathcal F \to \mathbb R$ lives in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$, the Banach space of bounded functions on $\mathcal F$ with the sup norm. Donsker's theorem is a Banach-valued CLT: $\sqrt n(P_n - P)$ converges in distribution (in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$) to a Gaussian process.

Prokhorov's theorem (tightness $\Leftrightarrow$ pre-compactness in distribution) is the probabilistic lift of Heine–Borel / Bolzano–Weierstrass. Donsker's theorem is proven via finite-dimensional CLT plus tightness; the tightness step is the compactness half of the argument.

The functional delta method and continuous-mapping arguments in empirical-process theory are $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ statements lifted to Banach-valued random elements. Continuity of functionals $T: D[0, 1] \to \mathbb R$ in the sup-norm metric is the key hypothesis.

Glivenko–Cantelli ($\sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} 0$) is the canonical uniform LLN. Donsker's theorem lifts this to a CLT uniform over function classes — the pointwise-vs-uniform distinction from formalcalculus is the foundation of the entire field.
Covering and bracketing numbers are metric-entropy constructions on $(\mathcal{F}, L^2(P))$; §32.6 uses the metric-entropy vocabulary introduced there.
§32.4's G-C-for-VC bound is the empirical-process core of PAC generalization bounds; formalML develops the learning-theory framing with Rademacher complexity and uniform convergence of risk.
PAC-Bayes lifts Topic 32's function-class complexity arguments to a posterior-over-hypotheses setting; McAllester's 1999 bound uses the same symmetrization technique §32.4 introduces.
Conformal prediction constructs distribution-free CIs via exchangeability rather than empirical-process asymptotics; the two meet at Topic 29 §29.5's DKW inequality and Topic 32's uniform bands.
M-estimator asymptotics — the modern nonparametric-plus-parametric-component framework — is built on local empirical-process theory (local Donsker, local bracketing), which §32.10 Rem 22 defers.

Targeted maximum likelihood, augmented inverse-propensity weighting, and efficient-influence-function methods all rest on the functional delta method (§32.7) applied to nuisance-parameter empirical processes.

Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko asymptotics for the maximum $X_{(n)}$ and the generalized Pareto; forward-pointed from Topic 29 §29.10 Rem 18, orthogonal to §32 but listed here for completeness of the formalML handoff.

The asymptotic alternative to finite-sample exchangeability arguments for prediction intervals. The §7.1 bootstrap discussion leans on Edgeworth expansions, §3.3 QR asymptotics use empirical-process limit theorems, and Theorem 5.1 appeals to uniform stability of empirical-quantile order statistics.

Quantile-regression Theorem 3 runs through Knight's (1998) algebraic identity plus an empirical-process limit of the rescaled QR objective; the argmin lemma is the continuous-mapping step. Theorem 4's restricted-eigenvalue argument and oracle inequality both use empirical-process tools (covering numbers, self-normalized concentration).

Statistical-depth §4.1 consistency (Donoho–Gasko 1992) and §4.3 Massé asymptotic distribution are corollaries of empirical-process theory. The Vapnik–Chervonenkis Glivenko–Cantelli theorem on the halfspace VC class — the structural prerequisite — and Donsker's theorem for the same class give the limit law in three lines via the functional delta method.

The Vapnik–Chervonenkis Glivenko–Cantelli theorem on VC classes is the foundational result connecting empirical-process theory to PAC learning. Donsker's theorem for VC classes gives the uniform CLT that underwrites VC-dimension generalization bounds; the symmetrization argument in §32.4 is the empirical-process side of the formalml vc-dimension topic's bound proofs.
The absolute convergence condition E[|X|] < ∞ ensures the expectation sum/integral is well-defined. Interchange of limit and expectation (dominated convergence) is used in MGF proofs.

The MGF expansion $M_X(t) = \sum \mathbb E[X^n]\,t^n/n!$ is a Taylor series. The proof that $M^{(n)}(0) = \mathbb E[X^n]$ uses term-by-term differentiation of the power series. The delta method is a first-order Taylor expansion $g(\hat\theta) = g(\theta) + g'(\theta)(\hat\theta - \theta) + o_p(1/\sqrt n)$.

Moment existence for heavy-tailed distributions is an improper-integral convergence question: $\mathbb E[X^k] = \int x^k f(x)\,dx$ exists iff the integral converges, which depends on the tail decay rate relative to the power $k$.

$\mathbb E[X] = \int X\,dP$ is a Lebesgue integral of the random variable w.r.t. the probability measure. Linearity, monotonicity, and the convergence theorems (MCT, DCT, Fatou) are the tools used to prove every expectation identity.

The expected value $\mathbb E[g(X)] = \int g(x) f(x)\,dx$ is the defining integral of probability. Variance, covariance, and all moments are expected values — hence all are integrals. The linearity and monotonicity of the Riemann integral are the algebraic foundation.

KL divergence is an expected log-density-ratio (§3.1 of pac-bayes-bounds), and the moment generating function of the empirical risk is the technical workhorse of every bound proof in §§4–6. Both depend on the expectation-and-moments machinery developed here.

The log-partition function's moment-generating properties use Taylor-expansion arguments. The relationship between $A(\eta)$ and the moment-generating function connects to power series — $A'(\eta) = \mathbb E[T(X)]$ and $A''(\eta) = \mathrm{Var}(T(X))$ are the first two Taylor coefficients.

The cumulant generating function $K(t) = \log M_X(t)$ has Taylor coefficients equal to the cumulants $\kappa_n$: $K(t) = \sum \kappa_n t^n/n!$. The exponential-family structure makes these derivatives tractable in closed form, and the mean-value-theorem remainder bound governs higher-order corrections.
The Fisher information I(η) = A''(η) defines a Riemannian metric on the parameter space. Natural gradient descent uses this metric for parameter-invariant optimization.
Every GLM requires an exponential family response distribution. The canonical link function is (A')⁻¹. Logistic, Poisson, and Gamma regression are instances.
Exponential family variational distributions enable natural gradient VI. The ELBO has a closed-form expectation when both the prior and variational distribution are in the same exponential family.

§22.3 Thm 3 (asymptotic normality of $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$) and §22.7 Thm 6 (deviance LRT $\to \chi^2_k$) both rest on multivariate Taylor expansions of the log-likelihood around the MLE. The $\sqrt n$ scaling in the asymptotic distribution is exactly the Taylor-series remainder bound.

The IRLS algorithm for fitting GLMs is Newton's method on the gradient of the log-likelihood. The score $\nabla_\beta \ell(\beta)$ and its Hessian are the engines of the fitting procedure; §22.3 Proofs 1 and 2 chain the gradient through the link composition $\boldsymbol\mu = g^{-1}(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)$ via the multivariate chain rule developed in the gradient topic.

§22.3 Thm 1's GLM information matrix $\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol\beta) = -\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{W}(\boldsymbol\beta)\mathbf{X}$ is a Hessian; Newton–Raphson / IRLS uses it to compute the update step. Positive-definiteness (from positive $W$ diagonal entries) gives local convexity of the negative log-likelihood, and the standard quadratic-form derivative $\partial(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x})/\partial\mathbf{x}$ from second-order analysis is the underlying matrix-calculus identity.

The GLM score involves $\partial\mu/\partial\eta$ (Jacobian of the mean w.r.t. the linear predictor), and the IRLS weight matrix $W$ contains $(\partial\mu/\partial\eta)^2$ terms. Under the canonical link these simplify, but the Jacobian structure is what makes IRLS general.

§22.10 Rem 25 forward-points: GLMMs add random effects $\mathbf{b} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$ to the linear predictor for clustered or hierarchical data. Topic 22 covers the fixed-effects-only GLM; the random-effects machinery requires Track 7's Bayesian foundations and is treated at scale on formalml.
Inverse-probability-weighted estimators, doubly-robust estimators, and TMLE all use GLMs as the propensity / outcome model components. §22.10 Rem 27 catalog-points; the methodology lives at formalml.

When $p \gg n$ the GLM design matrix is rank-deficient and ordinary IRLS fails. §22.10 Rem 28 forward-points to the high-dimensional treatment: penalized GLMs ([Topic 23](/topics/regularization-and-penalized-estimation) is the Track-6 entry) plus the minimax theory and double-descent phenomenon at formalml.

Stein's identity in §28.5 is integration by parts applied coordinatewise to $g(X) = X/\|X\|^2$; the full proof relies on the multivariate gradient of this gradient field. Empirical-Bayes estimation of hyperparameters uses gradient-based optimization of the marginal likelihood, and full Bayes via HMC needs gradients of the hierarchical log-posterior.

The hierarchical-model marginal likelihood $p(x \mid \phi) = \int p(x \mid \theta)\,p(\theta \mid \phi)\,d\theta$ integrates over the individual-level parameter $\theta$. Full Bayes integrates further over $\phi$; these nested integrals define the partial-pooling structure §28.6 develops.

§5's eight-schools example IS a hierarchical model with partial pooling. This topic develops the partial-pooling theory — when the hierarchical structure improves estimates over no-pooling and complete-pooling alternatives — that probabilistic-programming applies as an instance.
The horseshoe, regularized horseshoe, spike-and-slab, and R2-D2 priors are the continuous-shrinkage alternatives to the hierarchical-Normal prior that §28.6 develops. §28.10 Rem 23 pointer.
Mean-field and structured VI for hierarchical models at scale; stochastic VI (Hoffman et al. 2013) and black-box VI (Ranganath et al. 2014). §28.10 Rem 24 pointer.
Hierarchical priors over weights, MC-dropout, deep ensembles, SG-MCMC over NN posteriors. §28.10 Rem 24 pointer.
Dirichlet process, CRP, hierarchical DP, stick-breaking. §28.10 Rem 25 pointer.
MAML and hierarchical Bayes over task distributions; the machine-learning reading of §28's group-level hyperparameters. §28.10 Ex 14 pointer.
REML, lme4, Stan-style GLMMs, recommender-system random-effects structures. §28.8 Rem 20 pointer.

Rejection-region probabilities under both $H_0$ and $H_\theta$ are integrals of the sampling density over $R$. Power $\beta(\theta) = \int_R f(x; \theta)\,dx$ is a calculus-of-variations object in $\theta$.

Convergence in distribution is the language of asymptotic null distributions (§17.9). Consistency of tests — power $\to 1$ as $n \to \infty$ under any fixed alternative — is a sequences-limits statement.
The power function $\beta(\theta)$ is differentiated to characterize most-powerful tests (previewed in §17.4, full treatment in Topic 18). The score test uses $\partial_\theta \ell(\theta)$ directly.

Chi-squared and goodness-of-fit test statistics are $L^2$ norms of standardized residuals. Cramér–von Mises and Anderson–Darling statistics measure $L^2$ distance between empirical and hypothesized CDFs — the formalcalculus $L^p$-spaces machinery is the rigorous foundation.

The absolute-continuity assumption $P_1 \ll P_0$ in hypothesis testing means the null assigns positive probability to every event of positive alternative probability — precisely the hypothesis of the Radon–Nikodym theorem. Without it, likelihood ratios are undefined on positive-probability events.

Randomized experiments use t-tests and z-tests for average treatment effects; falsification and placebo tests are hypothesis tests for identification assumptions. §9.4's weak-IV-robust tests (Anderson–Rubin, conditional likelihood ratio) and §12's Rosenbaum sensitivity bounds are inverted from hypothesis tests of the null treatment effect; §11.4 CATE heterogeneity tests are tests of constant treatment effect.

The inferential apparatus — Type I/II errors, p-values, Wald and likelihood-ratio tests under normal asymptotics — carries directly to high-dimensional-regression's §10 debiased lasso, which produces a $\sqrt n$-consistent normal estimator. The PoSI undercoverage demonstration and debiased-lasso fix appeal directly to this topic's testing framework.

Provides the $H_0/H_1$ framework, type-I error, $p$-value definition, and level-vs-size distinction that every section of rank-tests deploys without redefinition. The permutation-test exactness theorem in §2 is a finite-sample analog of the level-$\alpha$ framework developed here.

PAC learning's $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-formulation in §6.1 of vc-dimension is structurally parallel to hypothesis testing's $(\alpha, \beta)$-power calculation; familiarity with the testing framework's tradeoffs provides the natural intuition for the sample-complexity bounds in §§7.1–7.2.

§30.4's bias derivation Taylor-expands $f$ around $x$ to second order; §30.6's optimization Taylor-expands AMISE around $h^\ast$. Both reduce to first- and second-order conditions on standard Taylor expansions.
§30.6 Thm 5 (Epanechnikov optimality) uses Lagrangian calculus-of-variations — the Euler–Lagrange equation on a quadratic functional with linear constraints.

KDE is a function-approximation problem — approximating the unknown density $f$ by convolution with a kernel at bandwidth $h$. Consistency rates depend on the smoothness class of $f$ (Hölder, Sobolev), and minimax rates for density estimation are approximation-theoretic results from the formalcalculus topic.
Uniform-consistency proofs for KDEs ($\sup_x |\hat f_n(x) - f(x)| \to 0$) use Arzelà–Ascoli-style equicontinuity and compactness arguments on the class of kernel-convolved densities.

The KDE's characteristic function is the product of the data's empirical characteristic function and the kernel's Fourier transform. Plancherel's identity $\int|f|^2 = \int|\mathcal F(f)|^2$ converts the MISE spatial integral into a Fourier-side integral, clarifying bandwidth-selection asymptotics.

Mercer's theorem expresses positive-definite kernels as inner products in a feature Hilbert space; the reproducing property $\langle K(\cdot, x), f\rangle = f(x)$ in an RKHS is the kernel-methods workhorse. Gaussian-process and RKHS methods for smoothing are Hilbert-space regression.

MISE $= \mathbb{E}\!\int (\hat f_n(x) - f(x))^2\,dx = \mathbb{E}\|\hat f_n - f\|_{L^2}^2$ is the squared $L^2$ distance between estimator and target. Optimal bandwidth minimizes this $L^2$ risk, and Sobolev-space norms control smoothness-adaptive minimax rates.
The MISE $\mathbb{E}\!\int (\hat f_n(x) - f(x))^2\,dx$ is a multi-dimensional integral over the support. The bias-variance decomposition uses Fubini to swap expectation and spatial integration.

The KDE bias expansion $\mathbb{E}[\hat f_n(x)] - f(x) = (h^2/2) f''(x)\,\mu_2(K) + O(h^4)$ is a Taylor series in the bandwidth $h$. The dominant bias term gives the asymptotic MSE; the optimal bandwidth $h^\ast$ balances bias$^2$ against variance.
Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression is the covariate-conditional extension of KDE: average $Y_i$ values weighted by $K_h(x - X_i)$. §30.9 Rem 17 pointer; full development forthcoming on formalml.

Fan–Gijbels 1996 local polynomial regression corrects KDE's boundary bias and generalizes to the regression setting. §30.5 Rem 9 name-checks the local-linear-at-boundary estimator; forthcoming on formalml.

Rezende–Mohamed 2015 normalizing flows replace the kernel-average-of-bumps with a learned invertible transformation of a simple base density. §30.10 Rem 20 pointer; orthogonal to classical AMISE theory.
Mean-shift clustering uses gradient ascent on $\hat f_h$ to find local modes — the KDE's stationary points *are* the cluster centers. §30.9 Rem 18 pointer; forthcoming on formalml.
Sugiyama–Suzuki–Kanamori 2012 two-sample density-ratio estimation, the foundation of covariate-shift correction. §30.10 Rem 22 pointer; forthcoming on formalml.
Limits for the n → ∞ asymptotics in the LDP statement and the Cramér rate function evaluation.

First-order optimization of the Chernoff bound over t (the tilting parameter). The Legendre transform I(x) = sup_t(tx − log M(t)) is a convex conjugate, requiring differentiation to evaluate. Taylor's theorem enters the Hoeffding lemma.
Taylor expansion of e^x and log(1 + x) in the sub-Gaussian characterization and the Hoeffding lemma. The MGF expansion M(t) = Σ E[X^n] t^n / n! from Topic 4.
Expectation integrals in MGF computations. The Cramér rate function involves a supremum over an integral expression.

Tail probabilities $P(X > t) = \int_t^\infty f(x)\,dx$ are improper integrals; the rate-function asymptotics in Cramér's theorem control the exponential decay of these tail integrals. The MGF expansion required for sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential classes lives in the formalcalculus improper-integrals topic.

PAC learning bounds use Hoeffding: $P(|R(\hat h) - \hat R_n(\hat h)| > \varepsilon) \le 2|H| \exp(-2n\varepsilon^2)$. Rademacher symmetrization uses McDiarmid's inequality, and the $O(1/\sqrt n)$ generalization rate for bounded loss classes originates from these concentration bounds.
Sub-Gaussian gradient-noise analysis justifies step-size schedules in SGD. Azuma–Hoeffding applies to the martingale formed by cumulative SGD gradient errors, giving non-asymptotic convergence rates.

Maurer's 2004 moment lemma (§4.2 Lemma 1) and the Cramér-transform machinery underlying §4's MGF-based bound chain are the canonical large-deviations tools. PAC-Bayes is a posterior-averaged refinement of Cramér's theorem — the Donsker–Varadhan variational form is large-deviations theory in distribution-over-hypotheses form.

Concentration inequalities (Hoeffding, McDiarmid) underwrite the per-class uniform-convergence bounds that feed the SRM penalty. The §3.1 derivation cites Hoeffding via the FTSL; the §5 Rademacher SRM cites McDiarmid via symmetrization-plus-McDiarmid.

Hoeffding's inequality and the Chernoff bound from large-deviation theory supply the concentration substrate that, combined with VC dimension's polynomial growth function via the union bound, produces the agnostic PAC bound in §6.

The SLLN is an almost sure convergence statement — P(lim X̄ₙ = μ) = 1 — which requires the formal definition of limits and the ε-N proof technique. Limsup and liminf appear in the Borel–Cantelli characterization used in the proof.

The Borel–Cantelli lemma — used in both the truncation step of Etemadi's proof and the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem — requires that Σ P(Aₙ) < ∞, a series convergence condition. The variance series Σ Var(Yᵢ)/i² < ∞ requires comparison tests.
The dominated convergence theorem is the key tool in the truncation argument: E[X₁ 1(|X₁| ≤ n)] → E[X₁] as n → ∞, and E[X₁² 1(|X₁| ≤ n)]/n → 0. Both limits are justified by DCT.

The strong LLN $\bar X_n \to \mu$ a.s. is a statement about the Lebesgue integral $\int X\,dP$: the time-average along a single sample path equals the ensemble average. The proof (Etemadi, Kolmogorov) uses Lebesgue-integral tools — dominated convergence, monotone convergence, Fatou — throughout.

The Glivenko–Cantelli theorem extends the SLLN from sample means to the entire empirical CDF: $\sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| \to 0$ almost surely. This is uniform convergence of a sequence of random functions — the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ uniform-convergence framework lifted to a stochastic setting.

SGD convergence under Robbins–Monro conditions ($\sum \alpha_t = \infty$, $\sum \alpha_t^2 < \infty$) is proved via the SLLN and martingale convergence. Polyak averaging — computing the running mean of SGD iterates — converges almost surely to the optimum by the SLLN.

PAC learning bounds are WLLN statements: $P(|\hat R(h) - R(h)| > \varepsilon) \le \delta$. Uniform convergence over hypothesis classes (Vapnik–Chervonenkis theory) extends the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem from indicators to function classes.

The Neyman-Pearson proof integrates the indicator-function inequality $(\varphi^* - \varphi)(f_1 - k f_0) \ge 0$ over the sample space to convert a pointwise statement into an expectation inequality. The non-central $\chi^2$ series in §18.9 is a sum of integrals against shifted-df Gamma densities.

Convergence in distribution (the Wilks conclusion $-2\log\Lambda_n \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_1$) and in probability ($\hat\theta_n \xrightarrow{P} \theta_0$) are both rigorous limit statements. The $O_P / o_P$ algebra used in Step 4 of the Wilks proof is formal bookkeeping for these limits.

The score test statistic $U(\theta_0)^2/I(\theta_0)$ and the Wald statistic $(\hat\theta - \theta_0)^2 I(\hat\theta)$ are both built from first and second derivatives of the log-likelihood. The asymptotic chi-squared distribution follows from a Taylor expansion around $\theta_0$.

The likelihood ratio $\Lambda(x) = f_1(x)/f_0(x) = dP_1/dP_0$ is the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the alternative w.r.t. the null. The Neyman–Pearson lemma — that the LRT is the most powerful test at any level — is proven using monotonicity properties of RN derivatives.

The Neyman–Pearson optimal test under correctly-specified parametric models — i.e., the $t$-test under normality — is the parametric foil against which rank-tests §5's ARE compares Wilcoxon. The ARE framework asks: how much power do we lose by giving up the parametric model?

§21.7 characterizes the hat matrix $\mathbf{H}$ as an orthogonal projector — idempotent, symmetric, with $\text{rank}(\mathbf{H}) = \text{tr}(\mathbf{H}) = p + 1$. The spectral decomposition of a symmetric idempotent matrix (eigenvalues $\in \{0, 1\}$) is the calculus-side fact the proof invokes. §21.8 Proof 9 uses Cochran's theorem on quadratic forms in Normal vectors to split $\text{SSE}_0 - \text{SSE}_1$ and $\text{SSE}_1$ into independent $\chi^2$ components.

The projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{X})$ — the OLS fit — is a bounded linear operator on $\mathbb{R}^n$ (a finite-dimensional Banach/Hilbert space). The operator-theoretic view generalizes to infinite-dimensional regression problems in nonparametric and functional-data contexts.

§21 Theorem 1 (OLS-as-orthogonal-projection) applies the projection theorem in finite-dimensional Hilbert space: OLS projects $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathrm{col}(\mathbf{X}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, a $(p+1)$-dimensional subspace under full column rank. The Pythagorean decomposition $\|\mathbf{y}\|^2 = \|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2$ underlies the ANOVA identity $\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSR} + \mathrm{SSE}$. The §21.4 matrix-form pivot rests on the normal equations $\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}$ expressing orthogonality of residuals to the column space.

Instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity — all live in the linear-model framework where OLS + identifying restrictions give unbiased causal estimates. §21.10 Rem 27 points here; the prerequisite is §21.4's matrix form and §21.8's inference machinery.

When $p > n$, $\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}$ is singular and OLS fails. [Topic 23](/topics/regularization-and-penalized-estimation) (ridge, lasso) is the Track-6 answer; the high-dimensional theory (double descent, minimax rates) lives at formalml. §21.10 Rem 28 states the forward pointer.

§21.6 Gauss–Markov (OLS as BLUE under homoscedastic errors) is the result mixed-effects §2.4's GLS-as-BLUE / Aitken whitening specializes: the whitening map $\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1/2}$ reduces GLS on the correlated-error system to OLS on a whitened system, and BLUE-preservation under whitening follows directly from applying §21.6 to the transformed design. Mixed-effects §2's GLS proof is therefore §21.6 plus a change of basis.

The OLS substrate this topic builds — normal equations, projection geometry, bias-variance decomposition, condition-number diagnostics — is what double-descent's classical $\sigma^2(k+1)/n$ U-curve specializes. The overparameterized regime extends the same decomposition with bias and variance components governed by Marchenko–Pastur integrals.

The kernel-regression §2.3 reframing of Nadaraya–Watson as degree-zero local polynomial regression draws directly on this topic's weighted-least-squares theory. §8.2's local-linear extension is locally-weighted OLS with intercept plus slope; its WLS solution generalizes the single-coefficient form via kernel-weighted normal equations.

Locally-weighted least squares with a degree-$p$ polynomial design matrix is the central machinery of local-regression. The $(X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y$ normal equations are the linear-regression formulas applied at every evaluation point, and the §3 equivalent-kernel formulation is the projection-onto-column-space picture from this topic read in kernel-smoothing coordinates.

Quantile regression's Theorem 3 asymptotic normality $\sqrt n(\hat\beta(\tau) - \beta(\tau)) \Rightarrow N(0, \tau(1-\tau)\, D^{-1}\Omega D^{-1})$ is the QR replacement of OLS's $\sqrt n(\hat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}} - \beta) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1})$. The Bernoulli factor $\tau(1-\tau)$ plays the role of $\sigma^2$; the density-weighted Gram matrix sandwich-replaces $(X^\top X)^{-1}$.

Sparse Bayesian regression specializes the linear-regression machinery of this topic to the $p > n$ regime where ordinary OLS is rank-deficient. The §10 diabetes benchmark builds on the linear-regression substrate established here — design-matrix algebra, noise-variance estimation, prior-on-coefficients framing — all inherited directly.

Parametric substrate for SRM's polynomial-regression worked example. The bias-variance decomposition and Gauss–Markov variance bound are used by name — the U-shape of MSE-versus-capacity is read off the parametric variance term $\sigma^2(k+1)/n$ from this topic's least-squares analysis.
Consistency is convergence in probability; the asymptotic-normality proof uses Slutsky's theorem and convergence of the observed information to the expected information.

The score function $U(\theta) = \partial_\theta \log L(\theta)$ is literally the derivative of the log-likelihood; observed Fisher information $J(\hat\theta) = -\partial^2_\theta \log L(\hat\theta)$ is the second derivative. The MLE $\hat\theta$ solves $U(\hat\theta) = 0$ — a derivative-equals-zero condition — and Newton–Raphson iterations use $J(\hat\theta)$ as the curvature scaling. The asymptotic-normality proof Taylor-expands the score around $\theta_0$.

The score vector $U(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \log L$ is the gradient of the log-likelihood. Gradient ascent on the log-likelihood, the geometry of the likelihood surface, and the steepest-ascent interpretation all apply directly to MLE.

Expected Fisher information $I(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}[\nabla^2_\theta \log L]$ and observed information $J(\hat\theta) = -\nabla^2_\theta \log L(\hat\theta)$ are Hessians of the negative log-likelihood. The asymptotic variance of the MLE is $I(\theta_0)^{-1}$; positive-definiteness of $I$ governs identifiability and curvature.

The implicit-function theorem justifies differentiating $\hat\theta(x)$ with respect to $x$ (needed for jackknife and influence-function calculations). The non-singular-Hessian condition at $\theta_0$ is exactly the identifiability condition.

Consistency and asymptotic-normality proofs for the MLE invoke the dominated-convergence theorem to interchange differentiation and integration (Fisher-information identities) and to pass limits through the log-likelihood.

Asymptotic normality of the MLE $\sqrt n(\hat\theta - \theta_0) \Rightarrow N(0, I^{-1})$ follows from a Taylor expansion of the score: $0 = U_n(\hat\theta) \approx U_n(\theta_0) + H_n(\theta_0)(\hat\theta - \theta_0)$, solved for $(\hat\theta - \theta_0)$ and rescaled.

The expected log-likelihood $\mathbb{E}[\log f(X | \theta)] = \int \log f(x | \theta)\,f(x | \theta_0)\,dx$ is an integral; the score and Fisher information involve integrals over the parameter-indexed density. Integration by parts and differentiation under the integral sign drive the asymptotic theory, with the MLE regularity conditions requiring interchange of derivative and integral — the same conditions as the CRLB in Topic 13.

Topic 14's general MLE small-sample bias theory — concretely the $(n-p)/n$ downward bias of the Normal-model variance MLE relative to the unbiased $S^2$ that divides by $n-p$ — is the prototype mixed-effects §4.1 invokes for variance components. The §4.2 REML correction generalizes the same degrees-of-freedom adjustment from a single residual $\sigma^2$ to the full random-effects covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma$, recovering Topic 14's correction as the fixed-design special case.

KLIEP's KL-divergence framing in §5.1 is built on MLE machinery — the constrained-MLE Lagrangian, the consistency theorem under misspecification, and the projected-gradient algorithm all reuse standard MLE technology applied to a ratio model rather than a density model.

The training objective in normalizing-flows §7 is plain MLE applied to a flow's parametric family. Consistency, asymptotic efficiency, the bias-variance tradeoff, and the consistency-under-regularity-conditions theorem all inherit directly from classical MLE theory; flows are a particular parametric family that supports closed-form gradient computation.

The §4.3 recovery of the Cramér–Rao bound when $\Lambda_\eta = \{0\}$ requires the standard MLE Fisher-information machinery. The semiparametric efficiency bound generalizes the inverse Fisher information of MLE to the inverse efficient information of a semiparametric model, with the worst-submodel Fisher information as the bridge.
The delta method uses the Jacobian of the moment-to-parameter map; the M-estimator sandwich formula uses partial derivatives of ψ(x; θ) with respect to θ.
The sandwich variance A⁻¹BA⁻¹ᵀ is a matrix product; positive-definiteness of the covariance of sample moments is a quadratic-form argument.
MoM consistency is convergence in probability inherited from the LLN; Slutsky's theorem appears in the asymptotic normality derivation.

Solving the moment equations $\mathbb E_\theta[g(X)] = n^{-1}\sum g(X_i)$ for $\theta$ is an instance of solving $F(\theta, \bar x) = 0$ for $\theta$. The implicit-function theorem gives conditions under which the solution $\hat\theta(\bar x)$ exists and is differentiable; its Jacobian w.r.t. $\bar x$ drives the asymptotic variance via the delta method.

M-estimation IS empirical risk minimization: θ̂ minimizes the empirical average of a loss ρ(X; θ), equivalently solves Σ ψ(X; θ) = 0 where ψ = ∇_θ ρ. Every ERM estimator with a smooth convex loss is an M-estimator.

Huber and Tukey M-estimators are the foundation of modern robust regression. The breakdown point and influence function quantify resistance to outliers. Huber loss is used routinely in ML for regression under heavy-tailed noise.

Quantile regression minimizes the check loss ρ_τ(u) = u(τ − 𝟙(u < 0)); its ψ is non-smooth but falls within the general M-estimation framework (modulo regularity). The scalar-intercept case is Topic 29 §29.4/§29.6; quantile regression is the covariate-conditional extension.

GMM (Hansen 1982) generalizes MoM to over-identified systems — more moment equations than parameters — solved by weighted least squares on the moment residuals. Previewed in §15.12 as the forward link.

Akaike's proof (§24.3 Proof 1) Taylor-expands $\ell(\theta)$ around $\theta_0$ in $p+1$ dimensions; the BIC-Laplace proof (§24.4 Proof 2) does multivariate Laplace with a Hessian determinant. Both rely on the second-order Taylor theorem with remainder.

TIC (Takeuchi IC) replaces the AIC penalty $2d$ with $\mathrm{tr}(J \cdot I^{-1})$ where $J, I$ are observed/expected Fisher information — both Hessians. BIC's asymptotic derivation uses the log-determinant of the Hessian at the MLE, and §24.5 Stone's proof leans on Hessian curvature.

Develops AIC, BIC, WAIC, and LOO as model-selection criteria; PSIS-LOO is the modern computational realization of LOO that stacking-and-predictive-ensembles uses, and the broader information-criteria context for the marginal-likelihood vs. predictive-density distinction lives in this topic.

§3 of variational-bayes-for-model-selection's Laplace-to-BIC asymptotic bridge specializes the classical-IC framework this topic develops; §13's alternatives section places VBMS alongside AIC/BIC/WAIC/LOO, all of which trace through here. The BIC penalty $-(d/2)\log n$ is the VBMS reference point.

When $p \gg n$, likelihood-based IC degenerates. Extended BIC (Chen–Chen 2008), stability selection (Meinshausen–Bühlmann 2010), and knockoffs (Barber–Candès 2015) extend the framework. §24.10 Rem 25.
Vapnik's SRM generalizes information criteria to function classes via VC dimension or Rademacher complexity. §24.10 Rem 26.

The formal definitions of almost sure convergence and convergence in probability are limit statements. The ε-N definition of limits (for sequences) is the template. Limsup and liminf appear in the Borel–Cantelli characterization of a.s. convergence.

The Borel–Cantelli lemma — the standard tool for proving a.s. convergence — requires that ΣP(An) < ∞, a series convergence condition. The first Borel–Cantelli is used in the proof that convergence in probability implies a.s. convergence along a subsequence.

Lp convergence is defined via the integral norm E[|Xn − X|^p] = ∫|Xn − X|^p dP. The dominated convergence theorem is used to interchange limits and integrals when proving that Lp implies convergence in probability.

Convergence in distribution $F_n \Rightarrow F$ requires pointwise convergence at every continuity point of $F$. The $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition of continuity is what this 'continuity point' qualifier means; the continuous mapping theorem directly composes $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ continuity with probabilistic convergence.

Dominated Convergence, Monotone Convergence, and Fatou's lemma are the trinity that justify interchanging limit and expectation. They appear in every convergence-of-estimator proof: 'by DCT, $\lim \mathbb{E}[X_n] = \mathbb{E}[\lim X_n] = \mathbb{E}[X]$.'

Almost-sure convergence $P(X_n \to X) = 1$ is a statement about a measurable event in the $\sigma$-algebra. Convergence in probability, $L^p$ convergence, and convergence in distribution are all measure-theoretic reformulations that reduce to the $\sigma$-algebra framework.

SGD convergence analysis is an exercise in modes of convergence. With decreasing step sizes satisfying the Robbins–Monro conditions, the iterates converge almost surely to a local minimum; with constant step size, convergence is only in probability to a neighborhood. Both regimes use the mode-hierarchy and Slutsky-style combination rules developed in this topic.

PAC learning bounds state that the empirical risk converges to the true risk in probability: $P(|\hat R(h) - R(h)| > \varepsilon) \le \delta$. The uniform-convergence version (over hypothesis classes) uses the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem — a.s. convergence of the empirical CDF.

The Bernstein–von Mises theorem states that the posterior distribution converges in total variation (hence in distribution) to a Normal centered at the MLE. This is the frequentist justification for Bayesian inference, and the mode hierarchy here is what makes that statement precise.

The $\sqrt{1/n}$ rate all PAC-Bayes bounds achieve in the agnostic regime is the standard rate of convergence in probability for sample means of bounded random variables — the canonical statement of modes-of-convergence at the rate that the kl-form and McAllester forms recover. §7 fast-rate refinements give $O(1/n)$ in the $L^2$-convergence regime.

The geometric-ergodicity statement for RMHMC and the relationship between trajectory length, effective sample size, and integrated autocorrelation time invoke the convergence-in-distribution and convergence-of-Markov-chains framework developed in this topic.

Consistency and CLT statements on the SMC weighted empirical measure in §10 of sequential-monte-carlo are stated in the vocabulary of weak convergence and $L^2$-convergence developed here; convergence in probability and in distribution are invoked without re-deriving the underlying machinery.

The asymptotic-exactness statement (§6.3 Welling–Teh schedule) and the $O(\eta + 1/B)$ bias bound (§8.3 Vollmer–Zygalakis–Teh) both rely on interpreting convergence in expectation versus convergence in distribution; the mode hierarchy of this topic is the right place to sort that out.
Proof 1 (Bonferroni) is the union bound applied once. The union bound on the event $\{V \ge 1\} = \bigcup_{i \in H_0} \{p_i \le \alpha/m\}$ is the only analytical tool Bonferroni requires.

Proof 3 (Holm) is an induction on the number of rejections $r$. The base case $r = 1$ reduces to Bonferroni; the inductive step uses the threshold $\alpha/(m - r + 1)$ on the remaining $m - r + 1$ hypotheses.

Every high-dimensional feature-selection procedure inherits a multiple-testing problem. BH is the default tool for selecting significant coefficients in deployed scikit-learn and R glmnet pipelines; §20.7 gives the theory, and §20.8 Thm 6 handles the positive-dependence regime regression inevitably lives in.

The Barber–Candès (2015) knockoffs framework is a direct descendent of BH: it constructs synthetic 'knockoff' features, computes test statistics per feature, and applies a BH-like step-up. The $\alpha \cdot \pi_0$ control of §20.7 Thm 5 is the result it generalizes. §20.10 Rem 28 states the forward pointer.

The single-test framework of §20.3 assumes the $m$ hypotheses and the stopping rule are fixed in advance. Always-valid confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021) and e-processes (Vovk 2019, Grünwald et al. 2024) dispense with this by using supermartingale / anytime bounds. §20.10 Rem 26 states the forward pointer.

The streaming generalization of BH — Javanmard–Montanari 2018 Online-BH and Ramdas et al. 2018 SAFFRON / LORD — allows hypotheses to arrive sequentially with FDR control at each time. §20.10 Rem 27 points forward to the full treatment.
The multivariate change of variables formula (§8) uses the Jacobian determinant. The whitening transform and Cholesky decomposition are special cases of affine changes of variables.
The spectral decomposition Σ = QΛQ^T gives the principal axes of the MVN distribution. Eigenvalues are the variances along principal axes. This is the mathematical core of PCA.

The multivariate change-of-variables formula for densities requires the Jacobian of the transformation. Polar-to-Cartesian, spherical coordinates, and linear transformations of the multivariate Normal all invoke Jacobian determinants — the formalcalculus jacobian topic provides the rigorous foundation.

A joint density $f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ integrates to 1 over $\mathbb R^n$ — a multivariate integral. Marginalizing $f_i(x_i) = \int f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\,dx_{-i}$ is an iterated integral (justified by Fubini); the multivariate-Normal normalizer $(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma}$ comes from the multivariate Gaussian integral.

A GP defines a joint MVN over function values at any finite set of inputs. The conditional MVN formula from §4 IS the GP prediction formula — conditional mean = posterior mean, conditional covariance = posterior uncertainty.

PCA is the eigendecomposition of the sample covariance matrix. The eigenvectors are the principal directions, and the eigenvalues are the explained variances. The MVN geometry from §7 makes this concrete.

The default variational family is the multivariate Normal — full-covariance or diagonal (mean-field). The reparameterization trick for VAEs uses the Cholesky sampling formula from §8: z = μ + Lε where ε ~ N(0,I).
Normalizing flows learn an invertible transform g from N(0,I) to a complex target. The change of variables formula f_Y(y) = f_Z(g^{-1}(y)) |det J| from §8 is the core mathematical tool.
Weight priors w ~ N_p(0, σ²I) are multivariate Normal. The posterior p(w|D) is approximately MVN for well-specified models. The Laplace approximation uses the Hessian as the inverse covariance.

§4 Thm 3's conditional-MVN formula $\boldsymbol\mu_{1|2} = \boldsymbol\mu_1 + \boldsymbol\Sigma_{12}\boldsymbol\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol\mu_2)$ (the Schur-complement reading) is the pure-probability identity mixed-effects §3 specializes to derive BLUP as the posterior mean $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{y})\,\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{y})^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}])$. Mixed-effects §2's marginal-distribution theorem reduces to the §3 affine-transform result here — linear maps preserve MVN.

The multivariate-Gaussian-kernel substrate (clustering §6.1) and the Mahalanobis-distance reading of GMM responsibilities (clustering §10.2) require the multivariate-normal machinery — covariance matrices, density form, marginal/conditional rules — that this topic develops.

Statistical-depth §3.1's Mahalanobis-depth construction and §5.1's DD-classifier optimality theorem both rest on the elliptical-symmetry framework articulated here. The depth-of-a-density connection — that depth functions reach their maximum at the density mode for elliptical distributions — is a direct corollary of §7's geometric picture.

Bahadur's proof (§29.6) Taylor-expands $F$ around $\xi_p$ and controls the remainder — the first-order term is load-bearing, the second-order term is $O(1/n)$. The Bahadur representation $\hat\xi_p = \xi_p - (F_n(\xi_p) - p)/f(\xi_p) + o_p(n^{-1/2})$ is a first-order Taylor linearization of the inverse-CDF map.

Joint densities of order statistics are multi-dimensional integrals; computing $\mathbb E[X_{(k)}]$ requires integrating over the $(n-1)$-simplex of order constraints. Marginal densities of individual order statistics fall out of these multivariate integrals via Fubini.

Split-conformal's quantile of conformity scores (Definition 7), QR's empirical conditional-quantile estimator (§3), and HL's Walsh-average ordering (§4) all rest on order-statistic theory. The asymptotic theory of empirical quantiles underlies the statistical guarantees in §§5–6 of prediction-intervals.

Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko trichotomy for the limit of properly normalized $X_{(n)}$. Topic 29 covers $\hat\xi_p$ at interior $p$; EVT covers $\hat\xi_p$ as $p \to 1$. §29.10 Rem 18 pointer; forthcoming on formalml.

Koenker–Bassett check-loss regression. Topic 29 handles the scalar-intercept case via §29.4/§29.6; quantile regression is the covariate-conditional extension. §29.10 Rem 19 pointer; forthcoming on formalml.
Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis. Permutation-distribution machinery is orthogonal to Bahadur asymptotics and deferred. §29.10 Rem 20 pointer; forthcoming on formalml.
Vovk–Gammerman–Shafer distribution-free prediction. §29.10 Rem 21 motivates via §29.7's quantile-CI perspective; forthcoming on formalml.
Tukey / Mahalanobis / halfspace depths — multivariate generalizations of the quantile function. §29.10 Rem 22 pointer; forthcoming on formalml.
Consistency is a convergence statement — θ̂ₙ →ᵖ θ or θ̂ₙ →ᵃ·ˢ· θ — which requires the formal ε-δ definition of limits and the convergence modes defined in Topic 9.
The regularity conditions for the Cramér-Rao bound require ∂/∂θ ∫ f(x;θ) dx = ∫ (∂/∂θ) f(x;θ) dx — interchange of derivative and integral, justified by dominated convergence.

The Cramér–Rao lower bound differentiates under the integral sign — a maneuver justified by dominated-convergence conditions. The delta method for estimators of the form $g(\hat\theta)$ is a first-order Taylor expansion: $g(\hat\theta) \approx g(\theta) + g'(\theta)(\hat\theta - \theta)$.

The mini-batch gradient is a biased estimator of the full gradient (if the batch is a strict subset); its variance is $\sigma^2/B$ for batch size $B$. The learning-rate schedule navigates the bias-variance tradeoff in optimization.

AIPW (§6), TMLE (§7), and DML (§8) are M-estimators / Z-estimators with augmented score functions; their asymptotic normality follows from the Stefanski–Boos (2002) M-estimator framework developed in this topic. The §4.3 sandwich-variance formula is the standard point-estimation derivation applied to causal estimators.

M-estimator / Z-estimator asymptotics — consistency, asymptotic normality, and sandwich-variance formula derived in §§6–9 of point-estimation — are the parametric substrate this topic builds the semiparametric framework on top of. The §10 sandwich-SE derivation is a direct lift.

CDF properties (Theorem 1) use limits at infinity and continuity of probability from Topic 1. The proof that F(x) → 0 as x → -∞ and F(x) → 1 as x → ∞ requires the convergence framework from formalCalculus.
The change of variables formula for PDFs (Theorem 7) uses the Jacobian and the substitution rule for integrals. The multidimensional version uses the Jacobian determinant.

Transformations $Y = g(X)$ of continuous random variables use the change-of-variables formula $f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,|\det J_{g^{-1}}(y)|$. The Jacobian determinant is the local volume-scaling factor that makes the density transformation law work.

A random variable $X: \Omega \to \mathbb R$ is by definition a measurable function — $X^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal F$ for every Borel set $B$. The $\sigma$-algebra $\sigma(X)$ generated by $X$ is the measurement resolution of $X$; every event involving $X$ is an element of $\sigma(X)$.

GPs are stochastic processes defined by their finite-dimensional joints; §2.2's Kolmogorov-consistency proof bridges from those joints to a probability measure on path space via the extension theorem. The PMF/PDF/CDF framework developed here is the substrate.

Normalizing flows learn invertible transformations of simple distributions. The change of variables formula f_Y(y) = f_X(g⁻¹(y)) · |det J_{g⁻¹}(y)| is the mathematical backbone — each flow layer applies this formula.
Fisher information is defined via the score function ∂/∂θ log f(x; θ), which requires the PDF parameterization. The statistical manifold is the space of distributions.
Variational inference approximates posterior distributions by minimizing KL divergence between density functions. The conditional PDF framework enables the ELBO decomposition.

§23.3 Thm 2 (lasso KKT) and §23.4 Thm 6 (coord-descent convergence) both rely on subgradient calculus and the optimality conditions for convex non-smooth functions. The subgradient of $|\beta_j|$ — single-valued $\text{sign}(\beta_j)$ for $\beta_j \neq 0$ and the interval $[-1, 1]$ at $\beta_j = 0$ — is the load-bearing convex-analysis fact. Tseng 2001's coordinate-descent convergence theorem requires the separability hypothesis $f = g + \sum_j h_j$ with $g$ smooth and each $h_j$ convex.

Ridge and lasso are $\nabla_\beta L(\beta) + \nabla_\beta P(\beta) = 0$ problems — penalized gradient equations. Coordinate descent and proximal methods for lasso are all gradient-adjacent optimization schemes.

Convexity of the penalized objective $L(\beta) + \lambda P(\beta)$ is a positive-semidefinite-Hessian condition. Ridge adds $\lambda I$ to the Hessian, strictly improving conditioning; lasso's subdifferential structure replaces the Hessian at non-smooth points.

Ridge regression minimizes $\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\|_{L^2}^2 + \lambda\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_{L^2}^2$ — the $L^2$ norms make the problem a closed-form projection. Lasso replaces the $\ell_2$ penalty with the $\ell_1$ norm, producing sparse solutions; elastic net blends the two.

§23.10 Rem 29 forward-points to the asymptotic theory under $p \gg n$: oracle inequalities, restricted-eigenvalue conditions (Bickel–Ritov–Tsybakov 2009), the lasso $\ell_2$-consistency rate (Wainwright 2019 Thm 7.13), debiased-lasso post-selection inference (Javanmard–Montanari 2014), and minimax bounds. Topic 23 stops at lasso $\ell_2$-consistency stated-only (§23.10 Thm 7); the proofs and tightness arguments live at formalml.

Modern overparameterized regimes (neural networks, random-features models) violate Topic 23's $p < n$ assumption. The double-descent phenomenon — risk curve as a function of model complexity has a second descent past the interpolation threshold — is treated at formalml. Implicit regularization (SGD's bias toward minimum-norm solutions) plays the role of explicit ridge in those regimes.

§7's high-dimensional sparse-regression case in semiparametric-inference uses the debiased lasso as the nuisance learner. The underlying Bickel–Ritov–Tsybakov rate $\sqrt{s\log p/n}$ for the lasso comes from the penalized-estimation theory developed in this topic, and the §23.10 Thm 7 forward pointer is what semiparametric-inference cashes in.

Sparse-bayesian-priors §5's Bayesian-LASSO comparison is the duality between $L^1$ penalty and Laplace prior developed in this topic. The horseshoe is the prior-side analog of adaptive shrinkage; §10's predictive-log-loss comparison places sparse Bayesian priors alongside lasso and ridge.

Tikhonov, ridge, and lasso are concrete instances of the soft-SRM rule (Definition 4) with capacity functionals $\|\theta\|_2^2$ and $\|\theta\|_1$ respectively. The implicit nested family is the parameter-space norm ball, indexed by the penalty parameter $\lambda$.
Continuity of probability (Theorem 6) uses convergence of partial sums. The proof relies on the same telescoping-sum argument and epsilon-N convergence framework developed in formalCalculus.

A probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal F, P)$ has $\mathcal F$ a $\sigma$-algebra and $P$ a probability measure on $\mathcal F$. Kolmogorov's axioms are measure-theoretic at base; the Carathéodory extension theorem from the formalcalculus $\sigma$-algebras topic is the bedrock that makes every construction here rigorous.

VC-dimension theory's $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-PAC framework is built on the same $\sigma$-algebra-and-probability-measure substrate as classical probability. The §1 sample-space rigor here is what makes PAC's 'with probability at least $1 - \delta$' statements well-defined as events on a product probability space.
The sigma-algebra and probability measure defined here generalize to abstract measure spaces. The Kolmogorov axioms are the probability specialization of the Lebesgue measure axioms.
Entropy H(P) = -sum p_i log p_i is defined on probability distributions over finite sample spaces. The axioms ensure that probability distributions — and therefore entropy — are well-defined.
The PKD proof cross-differentiates the log-factorization in the data argument and the parameter, deriving the separable equation that characterizes the exponential-family form.
Almost-sure equality in the Rao-Blackwell and Basu conclusions; asymptotic-sufficiency remarks in §16.12 use convergence in probability.

The factorization theorem and Rao–Blackwell proofs use joint-density integration and the interchange of integration with conditional expectation (Fubini). The PKD proof integrates a separable functional equation in both arguments; the Riemann-integral framework is the underlying machinery.

The information bottleneck method finds a compressed representation $T$ of the data $X$ that preserves information about a target $Y$. In the special case $\theta = Y$ and $T$ is the sufficient statistic, the bottleneck recovers the Topic 16 notion of sufficiency. Learned sufficient statistics are the non-parametric analog.

Self-supervised learning objectives (contrastive, masked-modeling) implicitly discover sufficient statistics of $X$ for downstream tasks. The Rao-Blackwellization intuition — that optimal estimators are functions of $T$ — reappears as the rationale for pretrained-feature reuse.

Variational bounds on the mutual information between $T$ and $\theta$ give tractable proxies for sufficiency in deep models. The exp-family structure from Topic 7 §7.7 gives the closed-form ELBO updates.

MDL codes data as parameter + residual; under exp-family sufficiency, the optimal parameter code uses exactly the sufficient statistic, making MDL and sufficiency operationally equivalent in that setting.
